Grass carp (Ctenopharyngodon idella) exhibit a remarkable capacity for somatic growth throughout their lives, with the largest recorded individuals attaining an ultimate total length of 150 centimetres [Li = 150 centimetres]. This prodigious size is accompanied by an extraordinary maximum body mass, with fully grown adults reaching an ultimate wet weight of 41,200 grams [Wwi = 41,200 grams], a value that reflects decades of continuous feeding on aquatic macrophytes. Field surveys of large riverine populations in the Yangtze basin have documented individuals exceeding this length, though such giants are becoming increasingly rare due to fishing pressure. The species' ability to convert plant material into somatic tissue so efficiently underpins its success as a controlled vegetation management tool, yet it also contributes to its reputation as a highly invasive species when introduced outside its native range. The growth trajectory from a tiny fertilised ovum to a massive adult is one of the most extreme among the Cyprinidae.

At the beginning of its life cycle, a newly hatched yolk-sac larva emerges from an embryonated egg measuring approximately 1.25 millimetres in diameter. This pelagic egg gives rise to a prolarva with a wet weight at birth of just 0.001 grams [Wwb = 0.001 grams], a miniscule initial mass that underscores the enormous size differential between the earliest life stage and the adult form. The chorion rupture event is succeeded by a brief endotrophic phase during which the yolk-dependent larva relies entirely on its endogenous reserves. After yolk-sac resorption and mouth opening, the larva commences exogenous feeding, typically on zooplankton, initiating a period of rapid growth that will continue almost unabated for years. The transition from a nearly invisible free-swimming larva to a fingerling capable of consuming aquatic vegetation represents a critical bottleneck in the species' early life history.

The onset of gonadal maturation in this species is closely tied to both body size and thermal regime. Individuals reared under controlled pond conditions at a stable water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C] typically attain puberty after 365 days since birth [tp = 365 days since birth], at which point they have reached a total length at puberty of 60 centimetres [Lp = 60 centimetres]. This length threshold corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 2,680 grams [Wwp = approximately 2,680 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions for the species. Field-caught specimens, however, exhibit considerable variation around this mean, with the length at first maturity ranging from 58 to 70.2 centimetres depending on local environmental conditions and population density. The attainment of reproductive competence is therefore not strictly age-determined but rather reflects a complex interplay between growth rate and thermal history.

Under the same thermal conditions used for maturation studies, maintained at 16 °C [T = 16 °C], the species demonstrates a maximum reproductive output that is truly staggering for a freshwater teleost. A single gravid female is capable of producing an average of 4,110 eggs per day [Ri = 4,110 eggs per day] over the course of a spawning season. This remarkable fecundity is facilitated by the semicystic ovarian structure typical of cyprinids, which allows for the continuous recruitment of oocytes throughout the reproductive period. The daily egg production translates into an enormous annual fecundity, with a single large female capable of depositing millions of semi-pelagic, non-adhesive eggs that drift with the current until they settle on submerged vegetation. This high reproductive capacity, combined with rapid juvenile growth and broad environmental tolerances, explains why grass carp have proven so difficult to contain once established in novel habitats.

The species' overall life span at 16 °C [T = 16 °C] is estimated at 21 years [am = 21 years], a considerable longevity typical of large-bodied cyprinids that allows individuals to experience multiple reproductive seasons and accumulate substantial somatic reserves. However, senescence eventually leads to a gradual decline in swimming performance and feeding efficiency, particularly in males, who may experience reproductive senescence before females. The oldest documented individuals from lacustrine populations in Russia have approached this upper limit, though most wild fish succumb to predation, disease, or fishing mortality well before reaching such an advanced age. The combination of a long maximum life span with an early maturation schedule and extraordinarily high fecundity places Ctenopharyngodon idella among the most productive freshwater fish species known to ecological science.
